subject: The Papyrus · How you move 100 million people
html:
The largest building site in the region is a transport map

A young, growing, still-spreading population has to get to work — and Egypt is pouring concrete and steel to make that possible. Cairo runs Africa's first metro (its first line opened in 1987), now three operating lines and more under construction, carrying millions of trips a day. (Source: Cairo Metro.)

Two headline machines

Two projects stand out. The Cairo Monorail's New Capital line runs about 54 km on 22 stations from east Cairo out to the new capital — among the longest driverless monorails anywhere — with passenger service that began in 2026. And the big one: a Siemens-built high-speed rail network of about 2,000 km, whose first ~660 km line will link the Red Sea at Ain Sokhna through Cairo to the Mediterranean at speeds up to 230 km/h. (Sources: Cairo Monorail; Siemens Mobility.)

The honest caveat, as ever with megaprojects: opening dates are targets, and big rail slips. But the direction is unmistakable — and it traces straight back to last month's number. A median age of 24 and a fast-urbanising country is why a nation builds three transport systems at once. The infrastructure isn't the story; the demographics underneath it are — the trains are just the demographics made visible.
